etymology: From Rome and “primacy” (Latin primatus, first place); the claim that the bishop of Rome holds supreme authority over the whole church as successor of Peter.
biblical_def: Roman primacy is the claim that the bishop of Rome—the pope—holds a supreme and universal authority over the whole church of Christ, as the alleged successor of the apostle Peter, to whom Rome assigns a primacy over the other apostles. The dictionary rejects the claim as without warrant in Scripture and contrary to the headship of Christ. The Lord forbade His apostles the very rank Rome assigns: “Be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.” Peter himself, far from claiming supremacy, calls himself simply “an elder” alongside the elders, and was openly withstood and blamed by Paul at Antioch—impossible if he held a supreme and unerring office over the church. The headship of the church belongs to Christ alone, whom God gave to be head over all things to the church, His body. The dictionary marks Roman primacy as a corruption built upon a misreading of the “rock” of Matthew 16: the rock is Peter's confession of Christ, or Christ Himself, the chief corner stone, upon whom the church is built—not a Roman episcopal throne. The claim grew over centuries by ambition, forgery (the False Decretals), and political opportunity into the papal monarchy the Reformation rejected, and was at last defined as papal infallibility. The dictionary holds that no man is the universal head of Christ's church; Christ alone is Head, the Scriptures alone bind the conscience, and the pretended primacy of Rome is the usurpation the Reformers called the church to forsake.
webster_summary: The claim that the bishop of Rome holds supreme authority over the whole church as Peter's successor; rejected as contrary to the sole headship of Christ (Ephesians 1:22) and the witness of Peter himself, who was a fellow-elder and was rebuked by Paul.

pos: noun phrase (a doctrine of ministerial lineage)
etymology: From “apostolic” and “succession” (Latin successio, a following after); the doctrine of an unbroken line of ordination and authority handed down from the apostles through the bishops.
biblical_def: Apostolic succession is the doctrine, held by Rome and the Eastern and Anglican churches, of an unbroken line of ordination and authority handed down by the laying on of hands from the apostles through an episcopal chain to the present clergy—so that valid ministry, and in the Roman view valid sacraments, depend on standing in that physical lineage. The dictionary distinguishes carefully. There is a true apostolic succession that Scripture commends: the succession of doctrine—the faithful handing-down of apostolic teaching from one generation to the next. Paul charges Timothy, “the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also”: a succession of truth, not of office-magic. The church is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the chief corner stone—a foundation laid once, not relaid in each generation. But the dictionary rejects the mechanical, tactile succession that grounds ministerial validity in an unbroken chain of episcopal hands rather than in fidelity to the apostolic gospel. Paul's own test of true ministry is doctrinal, not genealogical: though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel, let him be accursed. A church that holds the apostles' doctrine is apostolic, whatever its pedigree; a church that has departed from that doctrine is not apostolic though it can trace an unbroken line of hands. The dictionary holds that the Holy Ghost makes overseers and that the true succession is the succession of the faith once delivered—against the Roman use of tactile succession to deny the validity of Reformation churches and to bind the gospel to a lineage Christ never made the test.
webster_summary: The doctrine of an unbroken episcopal line of ordination from the apostles, on which Rome grounds valid ministry and sacraments; the dictionary affirms the true succession of apostolic doctrine (2 Timothy 2:2) but rejects mechanical, tactile succession as the test.

A church faithful to the apostolic gospel is apostolic, whatever its pedigree.

The corruption is the mechanical, tactile succession that grounds the validity of ministry and sacraments in an unbroken physical chain of episcopal hands, apart from fidelity to the gospel—and uses that chain to unchurch the Reformation congregations and bind grace to a lineage. The dictionary rejects it. Paul's test of true ministry is doctrinal, not genealogical: though an angel from heaven preach another gospel, let him be accursed. etymology: Lotario dei Conti di Segni, who reigned as Pope Innocent III (1198-1216); the pontiff under whom the medieval papacy reached the summit of its temporal and spiritual power.
biblical_def: Innocent III (reigned 1198-1216) was the pope under whom the medieval papacy reached the height of its temporal and spiritual power, claiming authority not only over the church but over the kings and kingdoms of Christendom. He asserted that the pope stood “lower than God but higher than man,” the vicar of Christ to whom emperors and kings must submit; he laid kingdoms under interdict and excommunicated rulers to bend them to his will; he presided over the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), which dogmatized transubstantiation; he launched crusades, including the Fourth Crusade that sacked Constantinople and the Albigensian Crusade against the heretics of southern France; and he approved the new orders that extended papal reach. The dictionary marks Innocent III as the very embodiment of the medieval papacy's pretension—the man of the papal office at its proudest exaltation, sitting as God in the temple of God, exercising the dominion over men that the Lord expressly forbade His servants: “the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them… but it shall not be so among you.” Peter had charged the elders not to be lords over God's heritage; Innocent made himself lord over kings. The dictionary applies its standing rule: it acknowledges his administrative genius and the genuine reforming zeal mixed in his reign, while naming the papal supremacy he embodied as the usurpation of the crown rights of Christ and the dogmatizing of transubstantiation as a deepening of the eucharistic corruption. Pride goeth before destruction; the papacy that climbed highest under Innocent was the very thing the Reformation, three centuries later, would call the church to forsake.

pos: noun phrase (a Roman tribunal of persecution)
etymology: From the Latin inquisitio, an inquiry; the Roman ecclesiastical tribunals established from the thirteenth century to detect and punish heresy, by force and the sword.
biblical_def: The medieval Inquisition was the system of Roman ecclesiastical tribunals established from the thirteenth century onward to detect, try, and punish heresy—employing accusation, interrogation, torture, and the handing-over of the condemned to the civil power for imprisonment, confiscation, or death, often by burning. Arising in the wake of the Albigensian Crusade and developed under successive popes, it was later extended in the notorious Spanish Inquisition. The dictionary names the medieval Inquisition as a grievous corruption of the church's nature and mission. The weapons of the church's warfare are not carnal: Christ rules His church by the Word and the Spirit, not by the rack and the stake. To compel faith by torture and to slay those judged heretics is to take up the sword Christ forbade His servants, and to do the very deed He foretold: “the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.” The Inquisition shed the blood of many who sought to follow Scripture against Rome—Waldenses, Lollards, and others before the Reformation, and Protestants after—so that the Revelation's vision of the woman drunken with the blood of the saints was read by the Reformers of papal Rome. The dictionary holds that persecution for righteousness' sake is a beatitude for those who suffer it and a damning sin for those who inflict it. The church is to persuade, not to coerce; to bless them that curse, not to burn them; and the conscience is bound by God alone, never by an inquisitor's fire. The Inquisition stands as a perpetual warning of what religion becomes when it weds the gospel to the sword.

etymology: From the Lord's word, “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Matthew 22:21); the principle of the distinct claims of the civil power and of God.
biblical_def: “Render unto Caesar” is the principle, grounded in the Lord's famous answer, of the distinct and ordered claims of the civil power and of God. When the Pharisees and Herodians sought to trap Him over the tribute money, Jesus called for a coin, asked whose image and superscription it bore, and answered, “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.” The saying establishes that the civil magistrate has a real and God-given claim—taxes, tribute, honour, lawful obedience—which the believer is bound to render, as Paul confirms: “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due… honour to whom honour.” Yet it equally establishes the limit of Caesar's claim: the things that are God's are not Caesar's. The coin bears Caesar's image and may be rendered to him; but man bears the image of God, and the worship, faith, and conscience of man belong to God alone, never to the state. The dictionary marks the doctrine against two errors. The first is the statism that lets Caesar claim what is God's—demanding the conscience, the worship, the ultimate allegiance that belong to God—against which the apostles answered, “We ought to obey God rather than men.” The second is the anarchic or sectarian spirit that withholds from Caesar even his lawful due—refusing taxes, honour, and ordinary obedience under a false claim of Christian liberty. The dictionary holds the Lord's balance: honour the king and pay the tribute that is Caesar's, but render to God the worship and obedience that are His alone, and when Caesar demands what is God's, obey God rather than men.
webster_summary: The Lord's principle of the distinct claims of the state and of God (Matthew 22:21): render Caesar his lawful due—tribute, honour, obedience—but render to God the worship and conscience that are His alone, never the state's.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordered distinction of the two claims. The first corruption is statism: letting Caesar claim the things that are God's. The coin bears Caesar's image and may be rendered to him; but man bears the image of God, and his worship, faith, and conscience belong to God alone. When the state demands the ultimate allegiance, the bowed conscience, or the worship due to God—as Caesars ancient and modern have—the believer must answer with the apostles, “We ought to obey God rather than men.” The state that claims what is God's has overstepped the bound the Lord Himself set.

The opposite corruption is the anarchic or sectarian spirit that withholds from Caesar even his lawful due—refusing taxes, honour, and ordinary obedience under a false banner of Christian liberty. But the Lord commanded the tribute rendered, and Paul confirms it: render to all their dues, tribute and custom and honour. The dictionary holds the Lord's balance exactly: honour the king and pay what is Caesar's, render to God the worship and obedience that are His alone, and when the two claims collide—when Caesar demands what belongs to God—obey God rather than men, and bear the cost.

pos: verb / noun (the error of the Judaizers)
etymology: From “Judaize” (Greek ioudaizo, to live as a Jew); the error of the Judaizers, who would compel Gentile believers to keep the law of Moses for salvation.
biblical_def: Judaizing is the error of the Judaizers—those teachers in the apostolic age who would compel Gentile believers to be circumcised and to keep the law of Moses as necessary to salvation, in effect adding works of the law to the grace of Christ. It arose early: “certain men which came down from Judaea taught the brethren, and said, Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved.” Against this Paul waged his fiercest battle, for it struck at the heart of the gospel. He withstood Peter to the face at Antioch for compelling the Gentiles to live as Jews; he warned the Galatians, “if ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing”; and he cried, “Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?” The dictionary marks Judaizing as the archetype of every legalism that adds human works to the finished work of Christ. It is not the honouring of the law in its proper place, nor the embrace of the Jewish heritage of the faith; it is the fatal addition of the law's works to grace as a ground of acceptance with God—and the apostle pronounces such a gospel accursed. The dictionary holds the doctrine against its enduring forms: the Roman gospel of faith-plus-works anathematized at Trent, the legalism that makes rules and observances the measure of standing before God, and every scheme that, having begun in the Spirit, seeks to be perfected by the flesh. The remedy is the gospel Paul defended: a man is justified by faith in Christ alone, apart from the works of the law, and to add anything to Christ is to lose Him.

corruption_paragraphs: Judaizing is the corruption to be named, the archetypal assault on the gospel of grace. The Judaizers would compel Gentile believers to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses as necessary to salvation, adding the works of the law to the finished work of Christ. Paul saw that this struck at the heart of the gospel and fought it without quarter: he withstood Peter to the face, warned that the circumcised seeking justification by law had fallen from grace and that Christ should profit them nothing, and pronounced any other gospel accursed. To add the law's works to grace as a ground of acceptance is to lose Christ.

The dictionary marks Judaizing's enduring forms. Its purest modern heir is the Roman gospel of faith-plus-works anathematized at Trent; but the spirit appears wherever rules, observances, or human performance are made the measure of standing before God, and wherever believers who began in the Spirit seek to be perfected by the flesh. The dictionary distinguishes this fatal addition from the lawful honouring of God's law in its place and from the embrace of the faith's Jewish heritage; Judaizing is neither. It is legalism at the root, and the remedy is the gospel Paul defended: justification by faith in Christ alone, apart from the works of the law—for to add anything to Christ is to lose Him.

pos: noun phrase (believing Jews and Jewish believers)
etymology: From “Jewish” and “Christianity”; the faith of Jewish believers in Jesus the Messiah, from the apostolic church to the present remnant—distinct from the Judaizing error.
biblical_def: Jewish Christianity is the faith of Jewish believers in Jesus the Messiah—the great body of the apostolic church, which was first wholly Jewish, and the believing remnant of Israel in every age since. The dictionary carefully distinguishes it from the Judaizing error. The Judaizers sinned by compelling Gentiles to keep the law for salvation; but the existence of believing Jews who, in the apostolic age, continued in many of their ancestral customs while resting wholly on Christ for salvation was no sin—James could note that among the believers were many thousands of Jews zealous of the law, and Paul himself observed Jewish customs as a matter of liberty and testimony, not of justification. The gospel came “to the Jew first, and also to the Greek,” and at every time there is “a remnant according to the election of grace” among Israel. The dictionary affirms several truths here. The church's roots are Jewish; the Messiah, the apostles, and the first church were Jews; and God has not cast away His ancient people, but preserves an elect remnant who own Jesus as Lord. Yet the dictionary holds equally that in Christ “there is neither Jew nor Greek… for ye are all one in Christ Jesus”: believing Jew and believing Gentile are one body, one new man, saved by the same grace through the same faith. The dictionary marks Jewish Christianity against two errors: the replacement view that despises the Jewish remnant and the heritage of the faith, and the opposite error—modern forms of which would make Jewish believers a separate, law-bound class, reviving the very Judaizing the apostles overthrew. The believing Jew is saved as the believing Gentile is, by grace alone, and the two are one in Christ.

The Judaizers sinned by compelling the law for salvation; but the believing Jews of the apostolic age, who kept many ancestral customs while resting wholly on Christ, did not sin—James noted the thousands zealous of the law, and Paul kept Jewish customs as liberty and testimony, not as justification. etymology: The dispute in the apostolic church, settled at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15), over whether Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved.
biblical_def: The circumcision controversy was the first great doctrinal dispute of the Christian church, settled at the Jerusalem council of Acts 15, over whether Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. Certain men from Judaea had troubled the Gentile churches, teaching that without circumcision they could not be saved; the question was carried to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem. There Peter testified that God had given the Spirit to the believing Gentiles as to the Jews, purifying their hearts by faith, and asked, “Now therefore why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they.” James gave the sentence: that the Gentile converts be not troubled with the yoke of the law, but asked to abstain from a few things for the sake of peace and conscience. The dictionary marks the circumcision controversy as the church's decisive, Spirit-led affirmation of justification by grace through faith, apart from the works of the law, for Jew and Gentile alike. Its enduring significance is twofold. It establishes the model of settling doctrinal disputes by the assembled elders searching the Scriptures and the testimony of God's working—a pattern for councils and confessions ever since. And it fixes forever the freedom of the gospel: the yoke of the ceremonial law is not laid upon believers, and any attempt to bind it again—the Judaizing the council overthrew—is a return to the bondage from which Christ has made His people free.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the live danger is re-laying the law's yoke (the Judaizing the council overthrew) and forgetting the model of settling doctrine by elders searching the Scriptures.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gospel freedom the council secured and the model of its settling. The circumcision controversy was the church's first great doctrinal crisis, and its resolution at Jerusalem fixed forever that salvation is by the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, for Jew and Gentile alike, apart from the yoke of the law. The enduring danger is the re-laying of that yoke—the Judaizing the council overthrew—wherever human works, rules, or observances are bound upon believers as necessary to salvation. To trouble those who from among the nations are turned to God with a yoke neither the fathers nor we could bear is to overturn the council's sentence and the gospel it defended.

The controversy also gives the church the abiding model for settling doctrinal disputes. The question was not left to private opinion nor to a single supreme bishop, but carried to the assembled apostles and elders, who searched the Scriptures and weighed the testimony of God's working, and reached a judgment owned by the whole church as agreeable to the Word. The dictionary marks this as the warrant for councils, synods, and confessions—not as authorities above Scripture, but as the church together submitting to Scripture to settle controversy. The freedom of the gospel and the ordered settling of doctrine were both secured at Jerusalem, and both are to be guarded still.

etymology: From circumcision, the Old Testament covenant sign, and baptism, the New; the question of their relation, central to the paedobaptist and credobaptist debate.
biblical_def: “Circumcision and baptism” names the relation between the Old Testament covenant sign of circumcision and the New Testament sign of baptism—a relation central to the debate between paedobaptists and credobaptists. The paedobaptist argues a continuity: circumcision was the sign of the covenant applied to believers and their infant seed, and Paul links the two in Colossians—“in whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands… buried with him in baptism”—so that baptism, succeeding circumcision as the covenant sign, may likewise be applied to the children of believers. The credobaptist, with whom the dictionary stands as a Reformed Baptist work, answers that the new covenant differs in this very point: circumcision was applied to the natural seed of Abraham, marking a mixed covenant people of believers and unbelievers, but the new covenant is a covenant of the regenerate, written on the heart, and its sign therefore follows faith, not natural birth. The true circumcision answering to baptism is the circumcision made without hands—the inward putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, that is, regeneration—and baptism is rightly administered to those who profess that faith, being “buried with him in baptism… through the faith of the operation of God.” The dictionary holds the credobaptist position while honouring the paedobaptist as a brother in the Reformed faith: the two agree that the covenant sign signifies and seals the righteousness of faith, as Abraham received circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had; they differ on the subjects—believers only, or believers and their infants. The dictionary marks the question as a real and weighty difference among brethren who hold one gospel, contending as friends over the New Testament administration of the covenant and its sign.
webster_summary: The relation of circumcision (the OT covenant sign) to baptism (the NT sign), central to the paedo/credo debate; the dictionary holds the credobaptist view—baptism follows faith, answering to the circumcision made without hands (Colossians 2:11-12)—while honouring paedobaptist brethren.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the matter is a weighty difference among Reformed brethren—paedo and credo—over the subjects of the covenant sign, not a corruption to be rebutted.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter is not a corruption but a real and weighty difference among brethren who hold one gospel. The paedobaptist argues a continuity between circumcision and baptism: circumcision was the covenant sign applied to believers and their infant seed, baptism succeeds it as the sign of the same covenant of grace, and so it may be applied to the children of believers. Paul does link the two in Colossians, and the argument is serious and Reformed. The dictionary honours the paedobaptist as a brother and does not treat his view as heresy but as an error of brethren on the administration of the covenant.

The dictionary, standing in the Reformed Baptist tradition of the 1689 Confession, holds the credobaptist answer. The new covenant differs from the old in this very point: circumcision marked the natural seed of Abraham, a mixed people of believers and unbelievers, but the new covenant is a covenant of the regenerate, written on the heart, whose members all know the Lord. Its sign therefore follows faith, not natural birth. The circumcision that answers to baptism is the circumcision made without hands—the inward regeneration—and baptism is rightly given to those who profess that faith, buried with Christ through the faith of the operation of God. Paedo and credo agree that the sign seals the righteousness of faith; they differ on its subjects, and contend as friends over the New Testament administration of the covenant.

etymology: From the apostle's phrase “the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2) and “under the law to Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21); the rule of life that binds the believer under the lordship of Christ.
biblical_def: The law of Christ is the rule of life that binds the believer under the lordship of Christ—the moral will of God as it comes to His people in and through their Redeemer. Paul names it directly: “Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ”; and he describes himself as “not without law to God, but under the law to Christ.” The phrase guards two truths against distortion. First, the believer is not lawless: though delivered from the law as a covenant of works and from the ceremonial yoke, he is not without law to God but bound to the abiding moral law, now established and deepened by Christ. The Lord summed it in the new commandment, “that ye love one another; as I have loved you”—not a lower standard than the old law but a higher, for love is the fulfilling of the law. Second, this obedience flows from a new principle: “the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death.” The believer keeps the law not as a slave earning wages, but as a son walking in the Spirit, with the law written on the heart of flesh. The dictionary marks the law of Christ against two errors. The antinomian seizes the phrase to abolish all law, as though grace freed the believer from the moral commands of God; but Christ came to establish the law, not to destroy it, and His law binds. The legalist, on the other side, would drag the believer back under the law as a covenant of works or under the ceremonial yoke; but the believer is under the law to Christ, kept by grace, fulfilling it by love and the Spirit. The law of Christ is neither lawlessness nor bondage, but the glad obedience of the free son of God.
webster_summary: The rule of life binding the believer under Christ's lordship (Galatians 6:2; 1 Corinthians 9:21)—the abiding moral law established and deepened by Christ, fulfilled by love and the Spirit; against both antinomian lawlessness and legalist bondage.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is obedience under grace—neither lawless nor enslaved. The antinomian seizes the phrase “law of Christ” to abolish all law, reasoning that grace has freed the believer from the moral commands of God, so that holiness is optional and the commandments passed away with the old covenant. The dictionary answers that the believer is “not without law to God, but under the law to Christ.” Christ came not to destroy the moral law but to establish and deepen it; His new commandment of love is no lower standard than the old but a higher, for love is the fulfilling of the law. The free son is bound to obey.

The legalist commits the opposite error, dragging the believer back under the law as a covenant of works to be kept for acceptance, or under the ceremonial yoke the gospel removed. But the believer keeps the law of Christ not as a slave earning wages but as a son walking in the Spirit, the law of the Spirit of life having freed him from the law of sin and death, the moral law written on his heart of flesh. The dictionary holds the balance: the law of Christ is neither the antinomian's lawlessness nor the legalist's bondage, but the glad, Spirit-wrought, love-fulfilled obedience of those whom grace has made free and sons.
